title: Acute Pericarditis and Myopericarditis: Diagnosis and Escalation

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with suspected acute pericarditis or myopericarditis in the emergency department (ED) or acute medical setting: diagnosis, risk stratification (high-risk features need admission), treatment of a first episode with colchicine plus aspirin or an NSAID, and escalation for tamponade, myocardial involvement or non-response. Source is the 2025 ESC guideline, with US product labels for medicine details. Not for incessant or recurrent pericarditis beyond the dosing table, constrictive pericarditis, post-cardiac-injury syndromes, or children.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi pericarditis guideline was found; the pathway follows the 2025 ESC guideline written for Europe.

Aspirin dose is from ESC Table 13 (750 to 1000 mg three times daily). The US over-the-counter aspirin tablet is 325 mg, so 750 mg cannot be given as a whole number of 325 mg tablets; the rounding to available strengths in Saudi Arabia was not verified.

The ESC colchicine dose is 0.5 mg; the only US 0.5 mg tablet label opened (Lodoco) is licensed for cardiovascular risk reduction and its dose is 0.5 mg once daily, and the generic colchicine tablet is 0.6 mg. No pericarditis-licensed colchicine label was opened.

The ESC text gives proton pump inhibitor gastroprotection without naming a drug or dose; esomeprazole 20 mg or 40 mg once daily comes from the Nexium label (risk reduction of NSAID-associated gastric ulcer, up to 6 months).
Ibuprofen US label is for arthritis; the pericarditis dose is from ESC Table 13. The label maximum daily dose was not extracted.
The cut-off for stopping NSAID dose in moderate or severe renal impairment is not given as a number by ESC (it says dose adjustment or corticosteroids).
Typical adult laboratory reference ranges are not taken from the guideline; laboratories differ.

pathophysiology.summary: Pericarditis is an inflammatory pericardial syndrome, with or without pericardial effusion (PEff); acute pericarditis has onset within 4 weeks (ESC 2025, Section 4.4.1). Most cases are presumed viral or idiopathic; the pericardium is electrically silent, so ECG changes mean the myocardium is also inflamed (ESC 2025, Section 3.3.2). Inflamed layers rub together, causing sharp pleuritic chest pain that improves on sitting forward (ESC 2025, Section 3.3.2). Pericardial effusion occurs in up to 60% of cases and is usually mild; a large or fast effusion can cause cardiac tamponade (ESC 2025, Section 4.4.1). Recurrence affects 20% to 30% of patients not treated with colchicine (ESC 2025, Section 7.2).

symptoms: Chest pain in 85% to 90%: sharp, pleuritic, better sitting up and leaning forward, worse on inspiration, lying down and swallowing (ESC 2025, Section 3.3.2).
Recent flu-like illness or gastroenteritis (ESC 2025, Table 6).
Dyspnoea, more common in older people (ESC 2025, Section 4.4.1).
physicalSigns: Pericardial friction rub in up to one-third of cases; it may disappear when effusion develops (ESC 2025, Section 4.4.1).
Electrocardiogram (ECG): PR depression early and widespread ST-segment elevation in up to 60% (ESC 2025, Section 4.4.1).
Signs of tamponade: low blood pressure, raised jugular venous pressure, pulsus paradoxus (ESC 2025, Section 4.5.4 and Table 17).
redFlags: Large pericardial effusion (more than 20 mm on echocardiography) or cardiac tamponade (ESC 2025, Table 16).
No response to aspirin or NSAID after at least 1 week (ESC 2025, Table 16).
Myopericarditis, immune suppression, trauma or oral anticoagulant therapy are minor risk features (ESC 2025, Table 16).
Raised troponin or new left ventricular dysfunction suggests myocarditis (ESC 2025, Section 8).
precipitants: Idiopathic or viral causes are the most frequent: 50% in inpatient settings and over 80% in outpatient settings in developed countries (ESC 2025, Section 3.4.2).
Tuberculosis, especially in people with human immunodeficiency virus infection in areas where tuberculosis is endemic (ESC 2025, Section 3.4.2).
Interventional procedures and cardiac surgery (post-cardiac injury syndrome) (ESC 2025, Section 3.4.2).
Systemic inflammatory or autoimmune disease, and cancer, especially lung, breast, lymphoma and leukaemia (ESC 2025, Section 3.4.2).
Autoinflammatory disease such as familial Mediterranean fever or tumour necrosis factor receptor-associated periodic syndrome in 5% to 15% of people with recurrence (ESC 2025, Section 3.4.2).
Trauma and oral anticoagulant therapy are minor risk markers for complications (ESC 2025, Table 16).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: ESC names ACS as the main differential diagnosis when troponin and ECG changes are present; rule it out with coronary angiography or coronary computed tomography (CT) when suspected (ESC 2025, Section 5 and Table 9).
Raised troponin with new impairment of left ventricular function suggests predominant myocarditis; troponin rise with preserved function is myopericarditis (ESC 2025, Section 8).
Listed by ESC among conditions that can mimic pericarditis with pleuritic pain; exclude by clinical probability and imaging (ESC 2025, Section 4.4).
Inflammatory pericarditis can present with pleural effusion and lung atelectasis that resemble pleuro-pneumonia (ESC 2025, Section 4.4.1).
Listed by ESC as a cause of pericardial effusion and tamponade; consider when pain is severe and effusion is present (ESC 2025, Table 8).

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm the diagnosis and exclude an emergency
actions: Take a history of pleuritic, positional chest pain; record pericardial rub, temperature and haemodynamics (ESC 2025, Section 3.3.2).
Record an ECG, send troponin, C-reactive protein, full blood count and creatinine, and do an echocardiogram (ESC 2025, Figure 7).
Rule out acute coronary syndrome (ACS) whenever indicated by the presentation, with coronary angiography or coronary CT as needed (ESC 2025, Section 5 and Table 9).

clinicalManagement.title: Stratify risk
actions: Look for fever above 38 degrees Celsius, subacute onset, large effusion over 20 mm, tamponade and no response to aspirin or NSAID after 1 week (ESC 2025, Table 16).
Admit anyone with one or more major feature and search for the cause (ESC 2025, Figure 7).
Discharge patients with no high-risk feature if they respond to treatment, with review within 1 to 2 weeks (ESC 2025, Section 7.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat tamponade and large effusion
actions: Cardiac tamponade needs urgent echocardiography-guided pericardiocentesis in a cardiology or cardiac surgery centre (ESC 2025, Section 6.3.2.1).
Use the clinical triage score: more than 6 points from at least two categories means immediate pericardiocentesis (ESC 2025, Figure 12).

clinicalManagement.title: Start anti-inflammatory treatment
actions: Give aspirin or ibuprofen at full dose every 8 hours, plus colchicine, plus gastroprotection (see medicines; ESC 2025, Section 6.2.2.1.1).
If aspirin and NSAIDs are contraindicated, use low-dose prednisone plus colchicine (ESC 2025, Section 6.2.2.1.1).
Continue the full dose until symptoms resolve and C-reactive protein is normal, then taper (ESC 2025, Table 13).
Advise restriction of physical exercise until remission, for at least 1 month (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 27).

clinicalManagement.title: Look for myocardial involvement
actions: If troponin is raised, check left ventricular function by echocardiography and consider CMR (ESC 2025, Section 8).
Raised troponin with reduced ejection fraction should be managed as myocarditis (see the myocarditis topic) (ESC 2025, Section 8).

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate and arrange follow-up
actions: Refer to cardiology for high-risk features, effusion needing drainage, myocardial involvement or no response (ESC 2025, Figure 7).
Review at 1 to 2 weeks and again after treatment; consider echocardiogram and C-reactive protein (ESC 2025, Section 6.2.2.1.1).

regimens.patientGroup: Adults with acute pericarditis, no ischaemic heart disease
regimens.dose: 600 mg to 800 mg orally three times daily (ESC 2025, Table 13). Tablets are 600 mg and 800 mg (Ibuprofen label, Section Description). Preparation: none; take with food.
regimens.duration: 1 to 2 weeks at full dose until symptoms resolve and C-reactive protein is normal, then decrease by 200 mg every 1 to 2 weeks (ESC 2025, Table 13)
adjustments: Normal or mildly reduced renal function: full dose; moderate to severe renal impairment: adjust the dose or use corticosteroids (ESC 2025, Table 13 footnote b).
Avoid in advanced renal disease and use caution in severe heart failure (Ibuprofen label, Section Warnings: Advanced Renal Disease and Heart Failure and Edema).
Avoid from about 30 weeks of pregnancy (Ibuprofen label, Section Warnings: Fetal Toxicity).
Give with a proton pump inhibitor (ESC 2025, Section 6.2.2.1.1).

monitoring: Blood pressure, creatinine and signs of gastrointestinal bleeding (Ibuprofen label, Section Warnings).
Symptoms and C-reactive protein to time the taper (ESC 2025, Table 13).
Echocardiogram for effusion if symptoms persist (ESC 2025, Section 6.2.2.1.1).
contraindications: Coronary artery bypass graft surgery setting (Ibuprofen label, Section Contraindications).
Aspirin triad: asthma, rhinitis, nasal polyps with aspirin sensitivity (Ibuprofen label, Section Contraindications).
Known hypersensitivity to ibuprofen or other NSAIDs (Ibuprofen label, Section Contraindications).

regimens.dose: 0.2 mg to 0.5 mg per kg per day orally (ESC 2025, Table 13); avoid higher doses except for a few days with fast taper to 25 mg/day (ESC 2025, Table 14 footnote). Tablets are 1, 2.5, 5, 10 and 20 mg (Prednisone label, Section Description). Preparation: none.
regimens.duration: 2 to 4 weeks at the starting dose, then taper over months: above 50 mg lower by 10 mg every 1 to 2 weeks; 50 to 25 mg lower by 5 to 10 mg every 1 to 2 weeks; 25 to 15 mg lower by 2.5 mg every 2 to 4 weeks; below 15 mg lower by 1.25 to 2.5 mg every 2 to 6 weeks (ESC 2025, Table 14)
adjustments: Taper only if asymptomatic and C-reactive protein is normal, particularly below 25 mg/day (ESC 2025, Table 14 footnote).
Offer calcium 1200 to 1500 mg/day and vitamin D 800 to 1000 IU/day to all patients (ESC 2025, Table 14 footnote).
Use caution in heart failure, hypertension or renal insufficiency (Prednisone label, Section Warnings).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Clinical presentation (typical pleuritic chest pain) plus more than one additional criterion: pericardial rub, ECG changes, raised C-reactive protein (CRP) or other inflammatory markers, new or worsening effusion, or pericardial oedema or late gadolinium enhancement on cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) (ESC 2025, Table 4 and Section 3.3.2).
Clinical presentation plus one additional criterion (ESC 2025, Table 4).
Clinical presentation only, without additional criteria (ESC 2025, Table 4).
Any major feature: fever above 38 degrees Celsius, subacute onset, large effusion over 20 mm, tamponade, or no response to aspirin or NSAID after at least 1 week (ESC 2025, Table 16 and Figure 7).
Definite acute pericarditis with raised myocardial injury markers and no new impairment of left ventricular function on echocardiography or CMR (ESC 2025, Section 8).

teaching.scope: Adults with suspected acute pericarditis or myopericarditis in the emergency department (ED) or acute medical setting: diagnosis, risk stratification (high-risk features need admission), treatment of a first episode with colchicine plus aspirin or an NSAID, and escalation for tamponade, myocardial involvement or non-response. Source is the 2025 ESC guideline, with US product labels for medicine details. Not for incessant or recurrent pericarditis beyond the dosing table, constrictive pericarditis, post-cardiac-injury syndromes, or children.
learningObjectives: Diagnose acute pericarditis with typical pain plus more than one additional criterion.
Stratify risk with the major features and admit high-risk patients.
Treat a first episode with an aspirin or NSAID, colchicine and gastroprotection.
pitfalls: Missing myocardial involvement when troponin is raised.
Starting corticosteroids first in a patient who could take an NSAID.
Missing a drug interaction with colchicine.
keyPoints: Colchicine for 3 months or more cuts recurrence.
Fever, subacute onset, large effusion, tamponade and non-response are high-risk.
Do not escalate corticosteroids for recurrence; add colchicine and an NSAID.
Restrict exercise until remission, at least 1 month.

patientEducation: Pericarditis is inflammation of the sac around the heart and usually settles within weeks.
Take the tablets exactly as prescribed, and keep taking colchicine for the full time.
Avoid hard exercise until your doctor says it is safe, at least 1 month.
Return urgently for worsening breathlessness, fainting or chest pain.
lifestyleAndDiet: Rest and avoid strenuous exercise until remission, at least 1 month.
Tell every doctor you are on colchicine before new medicines are started.
mdtReferrals: Emergency physician; cardiologist; echocardiography service; cardiac surgeon for drainage; clinical pharmacist for interactions; primary care.
dischargeCriteria: Pain controlled; no high-risk feature; troponin trend and echocardiogram reviewed; treatment and taper plan written; exercise advice given; review booked within 1 to 2 weeks.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at 1 to 2 weeks; repeat C-reactive protein and echocardiogram; taper per Table 13 when symptom-free with normal C-reactive protein; stop colchicine after 3 to 6 months; escalate for recurrence (ESC 2025, Section 6.2.2.1.1 and Section 7.2).
